1. A thyroid cancer history rules them out. If you or a close relative has had medullary thyroid cancer, or you have MEN 2, semaglutide and tirzepatide are not for you.
  2. A serious allergy rules them out too. That includes an allergy to any ingredient in the product.
  3. Some conditions need extra care, not a flat no. Past pancreatitis, gallbladder or kidney problems, diabetic eye disease and very slow stomach emptying all call for a careful talk with your doctor.
  4. Pregnancy changes the plan. Semaglutide should be stopped at least two months before a planned pregnancy, and tirzepatide can make birth control pills less reliable.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide help many people manage type 2 diabetes and weight, but they are not right for everyone. Their official labels name a small group of people who must not use them, and a larger group who need closer checks before and during treatment.

Below, we go through both groups, the rules around pregnancy and contraception, the questions worth asking your doctor, and the warning signs that mean you should stop.

What Are Semaglutide and Tirzepatide?

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are weekly injections used for type 2 diabetes and weight management. They belong to the same family, which is why their safety rules overlap so much.

Semaglutide, sold as Ozempic and Wegovy, is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. It copies a gut hormone that lowers blood sugar and slows how fast your stomach empties. We explain how semaglutide works in a separate guide.

Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, acts on two hormone receptors, GIP and GLP-1. That slower stomach emptying, shared by both drugs, is behind several of the cautions in this article.

The points below come from the US prescribing information for Wegovy (semaglutide, revised October 2025) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide, revised April 2026).

Who Must Not Take Semaglutide or Tirzepatide?

A “contraindication” means the drug must not be used at all. Both labels share the same core list. The table also includes situations where a label says a drug is not recommended or should be avoided:

Situation Semaglutide (Wegovy label) Tirzepatide (Mounjaro label)
You or a close relative has had medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) Do not use Do not use
You have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) Do not use Do not use
You have had a serious allergic reaction to the drug or any ingredient Do not use Do not use
You have severe gastroparesis (very slow stomach emptying) Not recommended Not recommended
You have attempted suicide or have active suicidal thoughts Avoid Not listed; discuss with your doctor
You are pregnant Stop once pregnancy is recognised, when used for weight or heart risk Use only if the benefit justifies the risk to the baby

The thyroid rule comes from the labels’ boxed warning: both drugs caused thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents. It is not known whether this happens in people, but anyone with a higher inherited risk of medullary thyroid cancer is kept off these medicines as a precaution.

The allergy rule covers more than the active drug. If you have ever reacted badly to an injection or a similar medicine, tell your doctor before you start.

Who Needs Extra Care Before Starting?

Many people with the conditions below can still use semaglutide or tirzepatide. The labels ask doctors to weigh the risk, monitor more closely, or adjust other treatment.

A Past Episode of Pancreatitis

Both labels warn that pancreatitis, inflammation of the pancreas, has occurred with these drugs. If you have had it before, your doctor will weigh that history carefully. Anyone who develops severe, lasting stomach pain on treatment should stop and get checked.

Gallbladder Disease

Gallstones and gallbladder inflammation were more common on semaglutide than on placebo, and both labels list gallbladder disease as a warning. Rapid weight loss is part of the reason, so a history of gallstones is worth mentioning.

Kidney Problems

The drugs do not usually harm the kidneys directly. The risk comes from dehydration when vomiting or diarrhoea is severe, which has led to kidney injury, sometimes needing dialysis. If your kidneys are already weak, your doctor may check them more often.

Diabetic Eye Disease

In people with type 2 diabetes, retinopathy complications were more frequent on semaglutide. Both labels say that anyone with a history of diabetic retinopathy should be monitored for progression.

Taking Insulin or a Sulfonylurea

Combined with insulin or tablets that boost insulin release, both drugs raise the risk of low blood sugar. Your doctor may lower the dose of those medicines when you start.

Other Medicines Taken by Mouth

Because both drugs slow stomach emptying, they can change how other tablets are absorbed. The Mounjaro label asks for extra monitoring with medicines where small changes matter, such as the blood thinner warfarin.

A Planned Surgery or Procedure

Both labels warn about a rare risk of inhaling stomach contents under general anaesthesia or deep sedation. Tell your surgeon, anaesthetist or dentist that you take semaglutide or tirzepatide before any planned procedure.

Pregnancy, Breastfeeding and Birth Control

If you could become pregnant, these drugs need a plan. The labels give clear rules for each stage.

Planning a Pregnancy

The Wegovy label advises stopping semaglutide at least two months before you plan to become pregnant, because the drug stays in the body for weeks. If you become pregnant while using it for weight management, it should be stopped once the pregnancy is recognised. For tirzepatide, the Mounjaro label says it should be used in pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the baby, so tell your doctor as soon as you plan a pregnancy.

Breastfeeding

There is not enough information on whether these drugs pass into breast milk. Both labels ask you and your doctor to weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against your need for the medicine.

Birth Control Pills and Tirzepatide

This rule applies to tirzepatide only. Because it slows stomach emptying, it can make birth control pills less reliable. For the background on its two-receptor action, see our guide to how tirzepatide works. The Mounjaro label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method such as condoms, for four weeks after you start and for four weeks after each dose increase.

Questions to Ask Your Doctor Before You Start

A short conversation before your first dose can rule out most problems. These questions cover what the labels ask doctors to check:

  • Does anyone in my family have a history of thyroid cancer or MEN 2? Ask relatives if you are not sure.
  • Could my past pancreatitis, gallstones or kidney problems be affected?
  • Do I need an eye check first? This matters if you have diabetes and any sign of retinopathy.
  • Should my insulin or diabetes tablets be adjusted?
  • Will this affect my other tablets? Bring a list of everything you take, including birth control pills and blood thinners.
  • What should I do if I plan a pregnancy?
  • I have a procedure coming up. What should I tell the team?
  • Which warning signs mean I should stop and call you?

Warning Signs That Mean You Should Stop

Even when the drug suits you at the start, some reactions need prompt medical attention. Contact your doctor straight away, or get urgent help, if you notice:

  • Severe stomach pain that does not go away, sometimes spreading to the back, which can signal pancreatitis
  • Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing, which can signal a serious allergic reaction
  • A lump in the neck, trouble swallowing or lasting hoarseness, which should be checked given the thyroid warning
  • Pain in the upper right abdomen, fever, or yellow skin or eyes, which can signal gallbladder problems
  • Vomiting or diarrhoea that will not stop, which can lead to dehydration and kidney strain
  • Low mood or thoughts of self-harm, which the Wegovy label asks doctors to monitor

Trouble breathing or a swollen throat is an emergency. For the other signs, contact the doctor who prescribed the medicine before your next dose.

Conclusion

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are not for anyone with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer, anyone with MEN 2, or anyone who has had a serious allergic reaction to them. Severe gastroparesis is another reason the labels do not recommend them, and the Wegovy label adds people with a history of suicide attempts or active suicidal thoughts.

For most other people, the question is how to use them safely. Past pancreatitis, gallbladder or kidney problems, diabetic eye disease, insulin or sulfonylurea use, other tablets and upcoming procedures all call for a careful talk with your doctor. If you could become pregnant, plan ahead: stop semaglutide at least two months before trying, and use a non-oral or barrier method of birth control around tirzepatide dose changes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I Take Semaglutide if My Mother Had Thyroid Cancer?

It depends on the type. A family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma rules out both semaglutide and tirzepatide. Other thyroid cancers are not on the contraindication list, but tell your doctor about any family history.

Can I Take Tirzepatide With Birth Control Pills?

Yes, but with a backup. The Mounjaro label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method, for four weeks after starting and after each dose increase.

Is Semaglutide Safe if I Have Had Pancreatitis?

Not automatically. Pancreatitis is a label warning for both drugs, so your doctor will weigh your history before deciding.

Can I Take Semaglutide While Breastfeeding?

There is not enough data to say. The label asks you and your doctor to weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against your need for the medicine.

Can I Use Semaglutide and Tirzepatide Together?

No. The Wegovy label does not recommend combining semaglutide with any other GLP-1 receptor agonist, and tirzepatide acts on the GLP-1 receptor too.

Do I Need to Stop These Drugs Before Surgery?

Tell your surgeon or anaesthetist that you take them. Both labels warn about a rare risk of inhaling stomach contents under anaesthesia, and your care team will decide what to do.
